title: Pennsylvania Central Airlines 105
summary: The aircraft approached Runway 18 from the north in a shallow descent that steepened near the approach end. Tower personnel observed it was too high and too fast. The aircraft touched down with only 1,500 feet of runway remaining and continued off the runway into Village Creek. The captain, first officer, and check airman perished; several passengers were injured.
probable_cause: The action of the pilot in committing himself to a landing from an approach which was too high and too fast.

factors.evidence: The flight approached Runway 18 from the north in a shallow descent that visibly steepened near the approach end
The aircraft touched down with only 1,500 feet of runway remaining
Considerable turbulence was experienced between Knoxville and Birmingham due to active thunderstorms
Mental and physical fatigue due to the late evening/early morning time of the flight and long length of the flight
The aircraft continued into Village Creek after turning off the runway

events.text: Flight 105 was cleared for a straight-in approach from the north by the Birmingham tower.
Flight 105 notified the tower it was performing a normal arrival pattern landing rather than the straight-in approach.
The last radio contact from the plane was received at 3:54 a.m.
Tower personnel observed the flight approach Runway 18 in a shallow descent that steepened near the approach end.
The aircraft touched down with only 1,500 feet of runway remaining.
The aircraft continued off the runway and crashed into Village Creek.

notes: CAB findings clearly documented probable cause
Weather and fatigue were contributing factors

title: American Airlines 6-103
summary: The aircraft descended below safe altitude in instrument conditions near Thing Mountain. After reporting position over El Centro at 8,000 feet, the aircraft did not respond to further contact attempts. The wreckage was found on the eastern slope of Thing Mountain at 4,870 feet, indicating an uncontrolled descent into terrain.
probable_cause: The probable cause was the action of the pilot in descending or permitting a descent to be made into instrument conditions to an altitude below that required to maintain clearance over Thing Mountain. The reason for the descent has not been determined.

title: 1946 Australian National Airways DC-3 crash
summary: Australian National Airways Flight VH-AET departed Hobart on March 10, 1946, with 21 passengers and 3 pilots, one of whom was a supernumerary pilot on his first flights with the airline. The takeoff was normal with both engines operating perfectly. Reaching about 400 ft, the aircraft turned left and descended steeply. It crashed into Frederick Henry Bay less than 2 minutes after takeoff, after flying only 2.9 nautical miles.
probable_cause: The investigation panel concluded the most likely cause was that the automatic pilot was inadvertently engaged shortly after takeoff while the gyroscope was caged. A subsequent inquiry by a Supreme Court judge discovered the captain was diabetic and kept this secret from his employer and the aviation authority, considering this condition probably contributed significantly to the accident.

factors.evidence: panel was satisfied that autopilot was inadvertently engaged shortly after takeoff while the gyroscope was caged
captain was diabetic and had kept it secret, judge considered his diabetes and self-administration of insulin probably contributed significantly
operation of the automatic pilot on-off control was not distinctive from operation of any other control in the cockpit
aircraft achieved normal climb of about 325 feet per minute before suddenly commencing descent of about 17½%

events.text: The return flight to Essendon Airport did not depart until 8:50 pm.
Observers at the aerodrome reported that the takeoff was normal, and both engines were operating perfectly.
Witnesses in the vicinity of Seven-Mile Beach estimated that the aircraft reached a height of a little above 400 ft before turning left slightly and descending steeply.
The panel members were satisfied that, after take-off, VH-AET achieved a normal climb of about 325 feet per minute before suddenly commencing a descent of about 17½%.
The aircraft cleared the land and crashed into Frederick Henry Bay about 300 yd beyond the water's edge and a mile from the western end of Seven-Mile Beach.

notes: investigation panel could not conclusively establish cause, identified autopilot engagement as most likely
Supreme Court inquiry examined three theories but found insufficient evidence for any one
captain's secret diabetes added posthumous contributing factor discovered after initial inquiry

title: TWA 513
summary: TWA Flight 513, a Lockheed L-049 Constellation operating a training flight on July 11, 1946 near Reading, Pennsylvania, experienced an in-flight fire when electrical wiring in the baggage compartment arced. The smoke and intense fire made it impossible for the pilots to maintain control.
probable_cause: Electrical wiring arcing in the baggage compartment creating fire in flight.

title: British European Airways 530
summary: The C-47 descended to approach Gardermoen airport in Oslo during clouds and low visibility. The aircraft passed the radio range station but subsequently struck trees on the eastern face of Mistberget mountain at 620 meters altitude while heading south parallel to the approach path. The crew was under pilot control at impact. Investigation found insufficient training in radio range navigation and equipment deficiencies contributed to the controlled flight into terrain.
probable_cause: Improper airmanship caused by insufficient training in radio range navigation combined with shortcomings in the aircraft's low frequency radio range equipment.

aircraft flew into trees on eastern face of Mistberget at 620 m altitude

title: 1946 Sabena Douglas DC-4 crash
summary: A Douglas DC-4 operated by Sabena crashed 35 km southwest of Gander, Newfoundland during approach in bad weather. The pilot attempted a visual approach and descended below the cloud base but struck trees in a dense wooded area, broke up and caught fire. The crash killed 27 people; 17 others were injured. The rescue involved the first large-scale helicopter operation.
probable_cause: The pilot did not carry out the appropriate approach procedure for landing in bad weather conditions.

events.text: The pilot attempted to carry out a visual approach in bad weather by trying to descend below the clouds.
Since the cloud base was about ground level, the plane crashed into trees in a dense wooded area, broke up and caught fire 35 km from the airport.
Unharmed survivors rescued injured victims from the burning wreckage, saving lives.
The United States Coast Guard launched a helicopter operation, the first large-scale use of helicopters in aircraft rescue, to evacuate the wounded from Dead Wolf Pond five miles from the crash site.

Aircraft registration OO-CBG confirmed from proving flight information

title: China Airlines 81
summary: Flight 81 departed Xichang at 13:45 on 20 September 1946 for Kunming. Communication was lost at 14:07 due to bad weather after the aircraft had climbed only twenty minutes. The aircraft crashed into mountains approximately 30 kilometers from Xichang. All 28 passengers and 3 crew members perished. The crash site was remote, difficult to access, and the search was hampered by poor weather and obstruction by local residents.
probable_cause: Aircraft lost contact shortly after takeoff in bad weather conditions; specific cause not determined from available information.

title: 1946 American Overseas Airlines Douglas DC-4 crash
summary: Flagship New England departed Stephenville at 4:45 AM bound for Berlin. Overcast skies blocked moonlight and starlight. Aircraft took off on runway 07 but instead of making required right-hand turn to avoid terrain, pilots continued straight. Seven miles from runway, struck ridge at 1160 feet and crashed.
probable_cause: Pilots' failure to make required right-hand turn immediately after takeoff, which led aircraft across terrain where insufficient clearance could not be gained.

title: 1946 KLM Douglas DC-3 Amsterdam accident
summary: The KLM Douglas C-47 was attempting to land at Amsterdam Schiphol in poor weather. The first attempt to land failed and the crew performed a go-around. The second approach to land also failed. On the third approach at approximately 300 feet, the engines appeared to have stalled, causing the aircraft to strike the ground and crash. All 21 passengers and five crew were killed when the aircraft caught fire and broke apart on impact.
probable_cause: Approach at too-low airspeed leading to a stall at insufficient altitude to recover.

title: 1946 Railway Air Services Dakota crash
summary: Dakota G-AGZA was de-iced and ready to depart Northolt for Glasgow on 19 December 1946 in a snow storm. After an hour-long wait for takeoff clearance, temperature dropped and snow refroze on the wings. When clearance came, the pilot took off with the aircraft almost entirely covered with snow. Unable to gain height due to ice contamination, the aircraft flew a few meters above ground down Angus Drive and struck rooftops of two houses, slewing 90 degrees to rest on the roofs. All 5 occupants and house residents were uninjured, but the aircraft was a total loss.
probable_cause: The pilot took off when the aircraft was almost entirely covered with snow, and the frozen snow on the wings prevented the aircraft from gaining height.

title: TWA 6963
summary: Lockheed L-049 Constellation crashed on approach to Shannon Airport, Ireland. During left turn onto final approach, the aircraft passed behind a low hill that blocked the airport lights from the pilot's vision. The aircraft lost altitude and the port wing tip struck the ground, causing the aircraft to crash and catch fire. Investigation determined incorrect assembly of static instrument pipelines and poor weather conditions contributed to the accident.
probable_cause: Incorrect assembly of the instruments static pipelines contributed. Poor weather conditions limited visibility and prevented the pilots from seeing the approach terrain.
